 Dengue toll hits 418, third-highest since 2000
 Published : 31 October 2026
 • 
 Updated : 31 October 2026, 16:09
 • 
 BANGLADESH
 SHARE 
 Helemul Alam
 Helemul Alam 
 Three more dengue-related deaths were reported yesterday, bringing this year’s death toll to 418, the third-highest annual toll since Bangladesh recorded its first outbreak in 2000. 
 According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), the highest number of dengue deaths was 1,705 in 2023, followed by 575 in 2024, 413 in 2025, 281 in 2022 and 179 in 2019.
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 A recent death review of 119 dengue patients by the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research, led by its director Quazi Ahmed Zaki, found that more than one-third died within 24 hours of hospital admission.
 The review identified dengue shock syndrome as the leading cause of death (62.5 percent), followed by expanded dengue syndrome (31.2 percent), dengue with bleeding (16.1 percent) and other causes (12.5 percent). Many patients also faced diagnostic delays of at least three days.
 Zaki said hospital-based death review committees examine each case and submit their findings to the DGHS’s Disease Control unit. The reviews assess causes of death, treatment quality, diagnostic delays, patients’ conditions before admission and the use of contraindicated medicines to identify gaps in patient management.
 Public health expert Mushtuq Hussain described the rising death toll as a failure of healthcare policy, calling for a shift from hospital-centred treatment to community-level interventions.
 He stressed the need for early diagnosis, proper patient care and secondary-level observation, with tertiary hospitals and intensive care units (ICUs) serving as the final stage of treatment.
 Mushtuq said low-income people often continue working despite having a fever due to financial pressures, delaying diagnosis until complications develop.
 He called for a functional three-tier healthcare system and suggested piloting free dengue testing at existing primary healthcare facilities, with vulnerable patients referred to hospitals when necessary.
 HM Nazmul Ahsan, associate professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, said many dengue patients were arriving in critical condition.
 “We are seeing a significant number of patients arriving in shock, with undetectable blood pressure and falling oxygen saturation,” he said.
 Ahsan said early treatment significantly improves recovery prospects for patients with dengue shock. Delays in transportation, emergency assessment and admission can cause irreversible organ damage and increase the risk of death.
 Ahsan said he had observed severe complications, including liver, kidney, respiratory and heart failure, as well as myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, among dengue patients this year.
 Such complications appear more common than in previous years, although further studies are needed to establish the reasons.
 He said the circulation of dengue virus serotype 3 (DENV-3) could be a contributing factor, as variations within a serotype may affect disease severity.
 Medicine specialist ABM Abdullah identified repeat infections and delays in diagnosis and treatment as major factors behind the rising death toll.
 Many of those who died might have had dengue previously, making them more vulnerable to complications from subsequent infections, he said.
 He urged people to seek medical advice and undergo testing if they develop fever and body aches rather than wait for their conditions to worsen.
 Prof Kabirul Bashar of the Department of Zoology at Jahangirnagar University said dengue deaths might not rise at the pace seen in October but were likely to continue in November, with only a modest decline.
 He stressed the need for intensified mosquito control, particularly indoors, where stagnant water provides breeding grounds.
